claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy has an FCC matrix.
The additively manufactured alloy contains a high density of intrinsic edge dislocations.
Elevated-temperature exposure causes Cr and Ti to migrate toward the surface, grain boundaries, and other defect sites.
Segregation of Cr and Ti at grain boundaries and dislocations governs protective-oxide nucleation and adhesion.
In the target alloy, Cr promotes formation of a protective Cr-bearing oxide scale under oxidizing conditions.
Ti contributes substantially to a coherent protective oxide scale in the target alloy.
Al2O3 may contribute to the protective scale formed by the target alloy.
The Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale initially slows further degradation and preserves alloy integrity.
Continued thermal stress and the high dislocation density eventually cause oxide-scale spallation.
Low oxygen activity in reducing gases prevents formation of a thick or coherent protective oxide scale.
Reducing conditions produce greater internal oxidation than oxidizing conditions.
Reducing conditions cause localized phase instability and microstructural degradation.
The as-manufactured dislocation structure is largely retained during exposure to reducing gases.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a relatively uniform Cr/Ti-rich oxide scale that subsequently shows spallation.
Reducing exposure will produce a much thinner oxide scale, or no external scale, relative to oxidizing exposure.
The starting alloy has high strength and strong fatigue resistance because of its FCC matrix and engineered dislocation microstructure.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 800–1000 °C and exposure times on the order of 100 hours.
Processing changes that alter dislocation density or grain-boundary character can modify or obscure the oxidation behavior.
Failure to observe Cr/Ti defect segregation or a systematic atmosphere-dependent difference in scale properties would falsify the proposed mechanism.
